description: Explorer-specific editorial notes refer to the shared local wine-style profiles. Descriptions are general tendencies, not promises for a particular bottle.

profiles.introduction: Often structured and fuller-feeling, Cabernet Sauvignon is a useful reference for a red with more noticeable tannin.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy dark-fruit flavours and a drying, grippy feel.

profiles.introduction: Merlot can range from supple and fruit-led to structured. It is a grape variety, not a guarantee of a soft wine.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want to explore plum-like fruit in a red, with body and tannin that vary.

profiles.introduction: Pinot Noir is often lighter in colour and tannin than Cabernet Sauvignon, but its body and flavour can vary widely.
styles: Still red wines, including regional appellations
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you like red-fruit possibilities and a lighter-feeling red.

profiles.introduction: Syrah and Shiraz are names for the same grape. Cool and warm settings can yield notably different expressions.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy dark fruit and might like peppery or savory notes.

profiles.introduction: Malbec is grown in several countries; Argentine examples are especially well known, while style still depends on place and producer.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want to compare dark-fruited reds with a fuller feel.

profiles.introduction: Grenache, also called Garnacha, is used in red wines and blends. Warmer sites can give riper fruit and more generous body.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you like ripe berry possibilities and less prominent tannin than some reds.

profiles.introduction: Gamay is the key grape associated with Beaujolais. Many examples are fresh and fruit-led, though cru and producer styles differ.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you would like to try a lighter red, sometimes served slightly cool.

profiles.introduction: Chardonnay is made in a wide range of styles, from lean and crisp to fuller wines influenced by oak or malolactic fermentation.
styles: Still white wines and sparkling blends
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want a grape that makes a useful comparison across regions and winemaking choices.

profiles.introduction: Sauvignon Blanc is often aromatic and fresh, but climate and winemaking affect how its fruit and herbal notes show.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy lively acidity and citrus or herbal aroma possibilities.

profiles.introduction: Riesling can be made from dry to sweet. Acidity, sweetness and fruit character are separate parts of the style.
styles: Still wines across a broad sweetness range
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want to learn how the same grape can produce different sweetness levels.

profiles.introduction: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are names for the same grape. Lighter, crisp examples and fuller, textured examples both exist.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you prefer an approachable white and want a useful lesson in regional style.

profiles.introduction: Chenin Blanc spans dry to sweet styles and can also be used in sparkling wines. Acidity often remains an important feature.
styles: Still dry, off-dry and sweet wines
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you like variety and want to compare sweetness and texture in one grape.

profiles.introduction: Gewürztraminer is aromatic. Its floral and spice-like aromas can seem bold, while the wine itself may range in sweetness.
styles: Still white wines, from dry to sweet examples
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy pronounced aromas; check the producer’s sweetness description.

profiles.introduction: Albariño is a Spanish grape often associated with fresh coastal white wines. Its profile varies with location and producer.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy fresh whites and often choose seafood.

sources.label: Rías Baixas DO on wines and Albariño

profiles.introduction: Grüner Veltliner is Austria’s best-known white grape. Styles range from light and fresh to richer examples.
styles: Still whites, with a broad range of weight
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you like fresh whites and want to explore an Austrian variety.

profiles.introduction: Rosé is a colour and style category, not a grape. Dry rosé can be made from different dark-skinned grapes and methods.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want a pink wine without assuming it is sweet.

profiles.introduction: Off-dry rosé has some perceptible sweetness, though its acidity and fruit aromas can change the overall impression.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you prefer a hint of sweetness; confirm the specific bottle’s description.

profiles.introduction: Champagne is sparkling wine from the Champagne region. Brut is a regulated sweetness category, not a grape or production method.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want to explore traditional-method bubbles with a dry style cue.

profiles.introduction: Cava is a Spanish designation for sparkling wines made under its rules. Traditional-method production is used, with permitted grapes and styles.
representativeRegions: Catalonia and other designated Spanish areas
styles: Traditional-method sparkling wine, with several sweetness categories
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you enjoy bubbles and want to compare a Spanish sparkling tradition.

profiles.introduction: Prosecco DOC is an Italian designation; many examples are made with Glera and use tank fermentation for their bubbles.
representativeRegions: Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you want approachable bubbles; check whether the label says Brut, Extra Dry or another category.

profiles.introduction: Moscato d’Asti is a lightly sparkling, typically sweet Italian wine. Bottles vary, so use regional designation and producer details.
profiles.whoMightEnjoy: If you prefer noticeable sweetness and gentle bubbles.
